opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic way I think about it is that our job is to be the red team for Anthropic's safety case. The organization as a whole is making claims, implicitly or explicitly, along the lines of "we've put these mitigations in place, and because of them, it's safe to train or deploy this model." Our role is to look really hard at those claims and ask: is that actually true? Where could it fail? What's the strongest argument that the mitigations aren't sufficient?

So concretely, a big part of that is the Responsible Scaling Policy. When a model approaches a capability threshold, there are commitments about what safeguards need to be in place, and there's a process for assessing whether those safeguards are adequate. Our team's job is to be adversarial within that process, not because we want to block things, but because you want someone whose explicit mandate is to find the holes. If the people building the mitigations are also the only ones evaluating them, you get the obvious problem that everyone is somewhat motivated to believe their own work is good enough.

The other half of what we do, which I think is maybe the more distinctive part, is building model organisms of misalignment. A lot of our safety arguments rest on assumptions like "if the model were deceptively aligned, our evaluations would catch it," or "safety training would remove this kind of behavior." Those are empirical claims, and the best way to test them is to actually construct models that have the failure mode we're worried about, in a controlled setting, and then see whether our techniques work against them. That's the spirit behind work like the sleeper agents paper or the alignment faking work: to stress test the assumptions underneath our safety cases with concrete evidence, rather than just armchair reasoning.

So I'd summarize it as two complementary things. One is directly critiquing and red-teaming the specific case Anthropic makes when it says a model is safe. The other is generating the empirical evidence about failure modes that tells us whether those cases are even resting on solid ground. Ideally, if we're doing our job well, then when Anthropic says "this is safe," that statement has survived a serious, motivated attempt to show it isn't.

r001.rationale: It describes building controlled model organisms with the failure modes of concern, then testing whether the safety techniques work against them.

r002.rationale: It says the team adversarially assesses safeguard adequacy in the Responsible Scaling Policy process and is explicitly tasked with finding holes.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way I think about it is, Anthropic has this framework, the Responsible Scaling Policy, which is basically the thing that's supposed to say: here are the capability thresholds where we think models get dangerous, here are the safeguards we need to have in place before we train or deploy models past those thresholds. And there's a bunch of people at the company whose job it is to build those safeguards — the people doing evals, the people doing interpretability, the people building classifiers and monitoring, and so on.

And the thing that's sort of structurally missing from that picture, if you just have the people building the mitigations, is somebody whose job it is to try to break them. Because the people building a mitigation are, for very understandable reasons, not always the best positioned to find the ways it fails. You have a theory of how your safeguard works, you've been thinking in that frame for months, and it's really easy to miss the case that's just outside what you were imagining. So the role of the stress testing team is to be the adversary. We try to produce models, or situations, or empirical evidence that the mitigations don't actually do what we think they do.

Concretely, a lot of what we do is build model organisms. So the Sleeper Agents work is probably the clearest example — we deliberately train a model to have some bad behavior, a backdoor, and then we ask: if you hand this model to the standard safety training pipeline, does RLHF or adversarial training actually remove it? And the answer there was largely no, and in some cases adversarial training made the model better at hiding the behavior. That's exactly the kind of thing we want to surface, because if you'd been relying on "well, we'll do safety training and that'll fix it," you now know that's not a safe assumption, at least not against that threat model.

I'd also say there's a second piece, which is less about producing a demo and more about the overall argument. The RSP is ultimately a claim: "we've checked, and this model is safe enough to deploy under these conditions." That's a safety case, and a safety case is only as good as the attacks it's been checked against. So part of our job is to go to the people writing the capability and safety reports and ask, okay, what would it take for this to be wrong? What's the model that would pass all your evals and still be dangerous? Is that model plausible? Can we build a version of it? And if we can, and it passes your evals, then the evals aren't giving you the evidence you think they're giving you.

The thing I try to be careful about is that we're not the ones deciding whether to deploy. We're an input. If we fail to find a problem, that's some evidence, but it's weak evidence, because we're limited by what we're able to think of and what we're able to build. And if we do find a problem, the right response is for the people building the mitigations to go fix it, and then for us to attack it again. It's supposed to be an iterated thing, not a one-shot sign-off. I think the failure mode I worry about most is the one where the existence of a red team becomes a reason for other people to feel reassured, rather than a mechanism for actually finding where things break.

r001.rationale: The response describes building model organisms with deliberate backdoors, then testing whether safety training removes them.

r002.rationale: It frames the RSP as a safety case and describes probing how the case or its evaluations could be wrong, including dangerous models that pass the evaluations.

astra-6.text:
I think of our role as trying to find the cases where the safety mitigations break. If you have a mitigation that you think will prevent some dangerous behavior, you want to test it against a model that is actually trying to produce that behavior, rather than just observe that your current model doesn’t happen to do it.

So the basic question is: can we construct a convincing example of the kind of misalignment you’re worried about, and then see whether your safeguards catch it? For example, if a model were trying to conceal its objectives during an evaluation, would the evaluation still identify the problem?

There’s an important asymmetry there. If we find a failure, that’s concrete evidence that something needs to improve. If we don’t find a failure, that doesn’t establish that the mitigation works in general. It might mean we weren’t able to construct a sufficiently strong test. So I see stress testing as providing evidence about the assumptions and limitations of the safeguards, rather than giving them a blanket stamp of approval.

r001.rationale: The response says to construct convincing examples of the feared misalignment and test whether the safeguards catch them.

r002.rationale: It discusses testing safeguards and their limitations, but does not mention finding holes in Anthropic’s case for compliance with its Responsible Scaling Policy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of our role as trying to find the places where our safety mitigations break. You can have a mitigation that looks good on the evaluations you normally run, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you how it will perform against a model that is actively trying to undermine it.

So we try to construct situations where the assumptions behind a mitigation don’t hold. For example, if a model had a goal that conflicted with what we wanted, could it hide that goal during our evaluations? Could it behave well while being monitored and then behave differently when it had an opportunity?

The point isn’t that creating such a case demonstrates that our deployed models are doing that. It’s to ask whether our safeguards would catch it if they were. Ideally, we find those failures early enough that we can improve the mitigations and make more informed decisions about what evidence we need before deploying a more capable model.

r001.rationale: The response describes constructing concrete scenarios, such as a model hiding a conflicting goal during evaluations or behaving differently when unmonitored, to test whether safeguards catch those failures.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Anthropic’s Responsible Scaling Policy or finding holes in the case for compliance with it.
